To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

socioeconomic position around birth and birth weight are negatively associated with caroid intima-media thickness in men and women, although the associations are not independent of adult lifestyle, and that socioeconomic position and lifestyle in adulthood are more important determinants of cardiovascular disease risk in middle age than socioeconomic position and birth weight around birth.
socioeconomic position at birth, birth weight, childhood socioeconomic position, childhood illness, and adverse events, and adult lifestyle were associated with carotidal intima-media thickness.

the risk of cardiovascular disease in middle age is strongly associated with adult lifestyle and biological risk factors but is only weakly related to socioeconomic position, birth weight, or other aspects of fetal life and childhood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of early life factors to health in later life, and in particular to the development of cardiovascular disease.
the effects of the early environment on later health and the mechanisms that mediate these effects.
the role of social and environmental influences in the development of disease in adulthood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
adult lifestyle and biological risk factors are the main drivers of cardiovascular health at mid-life.
the most important determinations of cardiovascular health at age 49 to 51 are adult lifestyle and biological risk factors.
early life events and adult socioeconomic status and lifestyle are important in determining the health of middle aged people.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a strong association between birth weight and carotid intimal medial thickness (CIMT) in men.
the early life environment, including socioeconomic circumstances, has a modest effect on the risk of cardiovascular disease.
the most important determinates of cardiovascular health are adult lifestyle and biological risk factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most important risk factors for cardiovascular disease are adult lifestyle factors and adult biological risk markers.
the risk for cardiovascular disease in adulthood is influenced by a combination of factors, some of which occur during early life, and some of which occur later on.
early life is not a major determinant of adult cardiovascular disease risk.
